claims.text: A machine-learned surrogate trained on ab initio free-energy data for both solid and fluid phases can accurately predict fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties of multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The surrogate can retain vibrational entropy contributions.
The surrogate can retain anharmonic free-energy effects.
The surrogate can retain electron–vibration coupling effects.
A surrogate trained on elemental and binary ab initio data can be applied to alloys containing up to five or six principal elements.
Atomic-configuration and local-chemical-environment descriptors encode the variables needed to predict phase free energies.
Learning the dependence of free energy on atomic configuration, composition, and temperature enables prediction of phase free energies without explicit molecular dynamics.
The proposed surrogate will be orders of magnitude faster than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics for multicomponent systems.
The proposed surrogate will be orders of magnitude faster than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Surrogate phase free energies will agree with explicit ab initio benchmarks to within a few meV per atom.
Derived fusion properties will retain fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio benchmarks.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows are accurate but computationally expensive.
TOR-TILD workflows for elemental and binary systems are accurate but computationally expensive.
The intended temperature domain extends from room temperature to temperatures above the melting point.
Model accuracy may degrade for compositions or temperatures far outside the training distribution.
Strong electronic correlations not represented in training may degrade model accuracy.
Transfer fidelity for electron–vibration coupling depends on the quality and representativeness of the training data.
